newsitem.title: USA: Health, religion groups seek "quality" in death.
newsitem.headline: Health, religion groups seek "quality" in death.

text.p: A day before the Supreme Court takes up the assisted-suicide controversy, 40 health, religious and retiree groups said Tuesday the whole debate over doctor-assisted deaths could be transformed if American medicine improved the quality of care for the dying.
Although the coalition includes such prominent foes of assisted suicide as the American Medical Association, not all the members formally opposed legalised doctor-assisted suicide.

But they all concur that the debate could be made irrelevant if Americans could count on end-of-life care that is "reliable, continuous, comprehensive and effective." They endorsed a 10-point programme for quality care for the dying ranging from pain management to helping bereaved relatives.
Led by the American Geriatrics Society, the coalition includes the AMA, the American Association of Retired Persons, the American Cancer Society, B'Nai Brith and the Catholic Health Association.

"No one needs to be alone or in pain or to beg a doctor to put an end to misery," said Dr. Joanne Lynn, a board member of the geriatrics group and a George Washington University professor who led a landmark study on how people died.

Her study published last year found that many people died alone, in pain and attached to machines. Their doctors often did not know their wishes for end-of-life care or whether they had do-not-resuscitate orders.

The U.S. high court Wednesday will hear two hours of arguments on whether mentally competent, terminally ill patients have a constitutional right to seek help from their doctors in committing suicide.

The dispute, which raises profound legal, moral and ethical questions, has sparked a debate of the most emotional intensity of any issue since the landmark 1973 ruling in "Roe v. Wade" that women have a constitutional right to abortion.
A court ruling is expected by July.
The coalition said the medical system, including Medicare and the managed care industry, should develop ways of monitoring the quality of end-of-life palliative and supportive care.
